SEC9A-01.my_answer: the barn owl, its nocturnal counterpart,
SEC9A-01.convention: paired commas around a nonrestrictive appositive; compound subject reaches plural verb
SEC9A-01.note: Solved independently: C. Options-only: C is the uniquely balanced option (comma both sides); A is the mismatched pair, B/D open and never close. A solver who knows 'marks must match' picks C without the passage.

SEC9A-02.convention: colon after an independent clause introducing an explanatory independent clause
SEC9A-02.note: Solved: A. Comma splice, fused sentence, and 'semicolon + because' are the three textbook wrongs; only the colon can be right. Options-only: the colon is the odd one out among {: , ;because none} and is the only mark that can join two clauses here. Demote to easy; standard module-1 fare.

SEC9A-03.my_answer: October, the figures for the river wards,
SEC9A-03.second_defensible: C would be fine if 'where...shifts' were restrictive, but the passage's comma before 'understate' forces a pair
SEC9A-03.convention: comma after a long introductory subordinate clause; paired commas around a nonrestrictive 'where' clause
SEC9A-03.note: Solved: B. The resolving mark is the comma before 'understate', six words past the blank, so it is not a four-word tell. Options-only: B is the only option with two commas, i.e. the 'most complete' pattern; a solver primed by A-01 picks it. Note the restrictive/nonrestrictive status of 'where' is only decided by that later comma, which is legitimate SAT design.

SEC9A-04.convention: closing dash of a dash pair; verb agrees with the plural head outside the supplement
SEC9A-04.note: Solved: D. 2x2 on mark x number, but 'were' appears in 3 of 4 options and the dash in 2, so majority-feature guessing lands on D. Passage 'two dissenters' makes the number trivial; the whole item is the dash-must-close rule.

SEC9A-05.my_answer: The supply ship having failed to arrive,
SEC9A-05.convention: nominative absolute set off by a comma
SEC9A-05.note: Solved: A. D is the best distractor (subject that never gets a verb). Absolutes are rare but attested on the digital SAT. Options-only: A vs B differ only by the trailing comma and a solver who knows a fronted phrase takes a comma picks A; still needs the finite/participle distinction to reject C and D.

SEC9A-07.my_answer: the two that remain intact are illuminated
SEC9A-07.convention: restrictive 'that' clause takes no commas; no comma between subject and verb
SEC9A-07.note: Solved: B. A ('that' inside commas) is an error no editor makes; C is a lone subject-verb comma; D has no verb. Options-only: B is THE ONLY UNPUNCTUATED OPTION and the only one that is clearly a finite clause, exactly the tell the brief warned about. Drop.

SEC9A-08.convention: semicolons between series items that contain internal commas, including before the final 'and'
SEC9A-08.note: Solved: D. Real convention and the distractors are real confusions. Options-only: D is the only option with a semicolon at both ends and a comma inside, i.e. the 'consistent' one; C is visibly over-semicoloned and A/B are mixed. Guessable as the balanced option.

SEC9A-09.second_defensible: C is left-dislocation ('the coral...it rarely colonizes'), a spoken pattern, not edited American English
SEC9A-09.convention: closing dash of a dash pair; subject reaches finite verb; comma before coordinating 'so'
SEC9A-09.note: Solved: A. Good distractor set (double subject, participle, mismatched mark). Options-only: dash in 3 of 4, bare finite verb in 2 of 4; A is the majority intersection.

SEC9A-11.my_answer: the physicist Lise Meitner, his collaborator of thirty years,
SEC9A-11.convention: restrictive appositive (no commas) followed by a nonrestrictive one (paired commas) inside a compound object
SEC9A-11.note: Solved: D. Structurally the same item as A-01 (appositive inside a compound, closed by a comma before the main verb, one mismatched-dash distractor, one unclosed distractor). Options-only: D is the uniquely balanced option again. Keep one of A-01/A-11, not both.

SEC9A-12.second_defensible: 'lime, that' is heard in speech; no style guide admits a bare comma between a fronted list and its summarizing pronoun (Chicago/CMOS wants a dash or colon)
SEC9A-12.convention: dash before a summarizing pronoun that resumes a fronted list as subject
SEC9A-12.note: Solved: C. 'was' right after the blank tells you the pronoun, not the list, is the subject, but you still need the dash rule. Options-only: the only dash among three comma/none variants, so the odd one out. Genuinely hard content, but the option set gives it away to a solver playing 'odd one out'.

SEC9B-01.convention: neither/nor: verb agrees with the nearer subject; head noun of 'the two surveys commissioned by the city council' is plural
SEC9B-01.note: Solved: A. Clean 2x2, no options-only tell. The comma distractors are style-only (weak); 'identifies' is the real one. Nearer-subject rule is on the CB list.

SEC9B-02.second_defensible: 'to whoever' — under prescriptive rule the pronoun is the object of 'judges' (judges [him] most likely), so whomever; MW/usage panels tolerate whoever but that is not the standard the test applies
SEC9B-02.convention: not...but parallelism (repeat 'to'); pronoun case fixed by role in its own clause
SEC9B-02.note: Solved: B. Grammatically sound and hard. AUTHENTICITY: who/whom and whoever/whomever case is NOT on the digital SAT's Form/Structure/Sense list (subject-verb agreement, pronoun-antecedent agreement, verb finiteness, verb tense/aspect, subject-modifier placement, plural/possessive nouns, genitive determiners). No Bluebook item tests it. Hold as off-list; do not ship as SEC hard.

SEC9B-03.convention: present perfect after 'ever since' + past point; 'along with' does not compound the subject
SEC9B-03.note: Solved: C. Two on-list mechanisms (tense, agreement past 'along with'), clean 2x2, nothing guessable from the four bare verbs. Best item in the batch.

SEC9B-04.convention: participle must modify the following subject; subject-case pronoun in a compound subject
SEC9B-04.note: Solved: D. 'the auditor and me concluded' is not a distractor an edited-English reader entertains. Options-only: D is the only option with 'I', the stereotyped correct form. Subject-modifier placement is on-list; I/me case is not. Drop: easy, off-list discriminator, guessable.

SEC9B-05.convention: plural subject past an interposed relative clause; not because...but because parallelism
SEC9B-05.note: Solved: A. 'but rather that' / 'but that' are audibly off, so the parallelism axis is weak and the item reduces to were/was with a singular 'newest' nearby. Fine, medium.

SEC9B-06.convention: closing comma of a parenthetical between subject and verb; singular 'delegation' governs the verb
SEC9B-06.note: Solved: C. Clean 2x2. Internal tell: every option contains 'it', which already tells the student the subject is singular, so the agreement half is given away by the option text itself and the item is really only the closing-comma rule.

SEC9B-07.convention: that-clause as subject takes a singular verb; closing comma of a parenthetical absolute
SEC9B-07.note: Solved: C. Genuinely hard: clause subject, two plural nouns in between, a long parenthetical to close. Clean 2x2, no options-only tell. Keep.

SEC9B-08.my_answer: but also the pattern books kept by its foreman offer
SEC9B-08.convention: not only...but also correlative; verb agrees with the nearer subject
SEC9B-08.note: Solved: D. The 'and'/'and also' distractors die on the passage's opening 'Not only', leaving offer/offers with singular 'foreman' as the trap. Sound; medium.

SEC9B-09.my_answer: the chief engineer, backed by two crews of local masons, was able to span the river
SEC9B-09.convention: participle modifies the following subject; verb agrees past an interposed plural modifier
SEC9B-09.note: Solved: C. Standard SAT combination (dangling modifier x agreement), clean 2x2. Medium, not hard.

SEC9B-10.convention: not only...but also joining parallel full infinitives; 'to' repeated because 'not only' precedes the first 'to'
SEC9B-10.note: Solved: B. Options-only: 'but also to + verb' is the stereotyped right form; 'as well as' and the gerund are transparent. Authored as medium; it is easy. Drop or park in the easy pool.

SEC9B-11.second_defensible: 'myself' as a compound object of 'to' is widespread but no style guide accepts it; not a second correct answer
SEC9B-11.convention: object case after a preposition in a compound; closing comma of a participial modifier before the main verb
SEC9B-11.note: Solved: C. The comma half is on-list; the I/me/myself half is not on the digital SAT list. Options-only: 3 of 4 have the comma, 2 of 4 have 'me'; C is the majority intersection. Hold as off-list.

SEC9B-12.second_defensible: 'whom' is the classic hypercorrection after an inserted 'the board believed'; prescriptively wrong since the pronoun is subject of 'had falsified'
SEC9B-12.convention: relative pronoun case set by role in its own clause across a parenthetical
SEC9B-12.note: Solved: D. Well built, and the resolving 'believed had' is 15 words out. But it is a pure who/whom item, which the digital SAT does not test; the old paper SAT tested it rarely at most. Hold as off-list.
